abstract_zh: 摘要 据报道,口腔卫生与流感感染之间存在关系。2019 年冠状病毒病 (COVID-19) 和流感是主要的呼吸道病毒感染。口腔可能充当这些病毒的进入位点和 储存宿主。本研究通过 流行病学 和组织病理学研究了口腔健康在 SARS-CoV-2 感染中的作用。还进行了一项前瞻性观察研究,以调查良好的口腔卫生习惯是否有助于预防呼吸道病毒感染。在使用健康/牙科检查和日本国民健康保险数据库数据的流行病学研究中,多变量分析确定口腔卫生不良是 COVID-19 发病的独立危险因素。组织病理学分析显示,有炎症的牙龈上皮中血管紧张素转换酶 2 (ACE2) 受体和弗林蛋白酶的表达高于没有炎症的牙龈上皮。这项前瞻性观察性研究比较了两组具有不同口腔卫生习惯的人群,结果表明,使用牙间刷和漱口水等良好的口腔卫生习惯可以预防 COVID-19 和流感的发作。总的来说,这些结果表明,不良的口腔卫生会增加 ACE2 和弗林蛋白酶的表达,从而导致 COVID-19 感染的发生。此外,改善口腔卫生可以预防 COVID-19 和流感的发作。

title: Spatiotemporal variations and influencing factors of highly pathogenic avian influenza risk in the Pan-Tibetan Plateau region
abstract: Abstract Background Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) is a major infectious disease threatening the poultry industry and public health severely. The spatiotemporal patterns and driving forces, however, remain elusive in the Tibetan Plateau and its vicinity, an ecologically critical corridor for migratory birds. This study aims to identify the factors driving these variations and to assess the HPAI risk in wild birds and domestic poultry across this region. Methods Based on HPAI records from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and the Official Veterinary Bulletin and 34 potential drivers in the Pan-Tibetan Plateau (PTP), comprising Xizang Autonomous Region (XZ), Qinghai Province (QH), Gansu Province (GS), Sichuan Province (SC), Yunnan Province (YN) and Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region (XJ), this study utilized the MaxEnt models to simulate spatial patterns of HPAI risk of wild birds, domestic poultry, and the integration of both, and identify key risk factors. Results Performances of models for wild birds and domestic poultry models were robust (both Test AUC values > 0.9). Although the mixed model performed acceptably overall, it significantly underestimated the infection risk in wild birds. High-risk areas of wild birds HPAI were concentrated in XZ, QH, GS and XJ (> 93%), showing a close relationship with natural factors like slope and distance to water sources. Conversely, those for domestic poultry were mainly distributed in YN, SC, GS (about 70%) and the peripheries of provincial capitals, dominated by socioeconomic variables such as gross domestic product and road networks. Moreover, overlapping HPAI risk areas were found in GS, XJ, XZ, and QH, which may be associated with increasing poultry production and fragmented wetland landscape. Additionally, it’s recommended that HPAI risk modeling be stratified by host types, particularly in areas with sparse surveillance data. Conclusions HPAI risks in wild birds and domestic poultry are dominated by natural factors and socioeconomic conditions respectively, and overlapping high-risk areas require focused attention. This study contributes to the understanding of HPAI transmission mechanisms in different hosts, providing a scientific basis for differentiated surveillance in the PTP.

title: Complementing Biosafety Levels With Societal Safety Levels
abstract: Biosafety level (BSL) classifications of biological agents have succeeded at minimizing occupational risk inside laboratories, but largely neglect the potential for onward transmission. As a result, many non-transmissible pathogens that could kill at most one individual per person exposed require greater containment than 1918 influenza, a virus that killed 50-100 million and might cause a new pandemic today. Laboratory workers are consenting professionals; the public is not. We recommend complementing BSLs with explicit thresholds for expected societal harm. Here we formalize Societal Safety Levels (SSLs) based on expected public fatalities per year, which we quantify from (i) estimated probability of laboratory release, (ii) likelihood of societal transmission, and (iii) consequence. SSLs would apply specifically to laboratory research with replication-competent potential pandemic pathogens, and would not restrict field surveillance, sequencing, or countermeasure development using non-replicating systems or pandemic-incapable agents. We find that applying the 0.1 expected deaths per facility-year standard common across multiple major-hazard industries to potential pandemic pathogen research would require marked safety improvements. Complementing BSLs with SSLs would establish enforceable accident-safety thresholds for pandemic-capable pathogens, bringing high-risk biological research into alignment with the quantitative safety standards that help other hazardous industries operate with public acceptance.

title: Rare Adenoviral Vectored Vaccines for Emerging Influenza Threats
abstract: Background: Emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases pose a growing global threat, underscoring the need for vaccine platforms enabling rapid deployment and durable, broad protection. Although mRNA and viral vector vaccines transformed pandemic responses, limitations include waning immunity, restricted antigenic breadth, pre-existing vector immunity, and rare vector-associated adverse events. Here, we evaluate recombinant adenovirus serotypes 4, 28, and 48 expressing a centralized H5 influenza hemagglutinin consensus antigen as next-generation vectors for broad, single-dose protection against diverse H5 influenza clades. Methods: An H5 centralized consensus vaccine was designed using human sequences from the 2003–2006 bird flu outbreak and cloned into four low-prevalence recombinant adenoviruses. Mice received a single intramuscular or intranasal vaccination and were challenged two weeks later with high doses of diverse, lethal, reverse-genetics-derived H5N1 viruses. Immune correlates, survival, and protection from challenge-associated weight loss were assessed. Results: Vaccinated mice were largely protected from lethal challenge against strains spanning twenty years of influenza evolution. Both vaccination routes conferred complete protection against antigenically related strains, and strong protection against more divergent clade 2.3.4.4b strains. Protection occurred before neutralizing antibodies could be detected, although strong H5 antibody responses were induced by all vaccines. Intramuscular vaccination generated strong serum IgG and antigen-specific T cell responses, while intranasal vaccination promoted robust antigen-specific mucosal IgA production. Conclusions: Adenovirus vectors expressing a centralized H5 consensus hemagglutinin elicit rapid, broad protection against diverse H5 influenza viruses following a single intramuscular or intranasal immunization. These results support the continued development of low-seroprevalence adenoviral vectors as a next-generation influenza vaccine platform for rapidly emerging influenza viruses.

Here, we evaluate recombinant adenovirus serotypes 4, 28, and 48 expressing a centralized H5 influenza hemagglutinin consensus antigen as next-generation vectors for broad, single-dose protection against diverse H5 influenza clades. Methods: An H5 centralized consensus vaccine was designed using human sequences from the 2003–2006 bird flu outbreak and cloned into four low-prevalence recombinant adenoviruses. Mice received a single intramuscular or intranasal vaccination and were challenged two weeks later with high doses of diverse, lethal, reverse-genetics-derived H5N1 viruses. Immune correlates, survival, and protection from challenge-associated weight loss were assessed. Results: Vaccinated mice were largely protected from lethal challenge against strains spanning twenty years of influenza evolution. Both vaccination routes conferred complete protection against antigenically related strains, and strong protection against more divergent clade 2.3.4.4b strains. Protection occurred before neutralizing antibodies could be detected, although strong H5 antibody responses were induced by all vaccines. Intramuscular vaccination generated strong serum IgG and antigen-specific T cell responses, while intranasal vaccination promoted robust antigen-specific mucosal IgA production. Conclusions: Adenovirus vectors expressing a centralized H5 consensus hemagglutinin elicit rapid, broad protection against diverse H5 influenza viruses following a single intramuscular or intranasal immunization. These results support the continued development of low-seroprevalence adenoviral vectors as a next-generation influenza vaccine platform for rapidly emerging influenza viruses.

title: A glycoengineered yeast-derived HA1-ferritin nanoparticle vaccine confers protective immunity against H7 avian influenza in chickens
abstract: Abstract H7 subtype avian influenza virus is an important zoonotic pathogen threatening the poultry industry and public health. Recombinant subunit vaccines provide a safer alternative to conventional inactivated vaccines, while yeast expression systems offer advantages of low cost, scalability, and engineering flexibility. However, their application in avian influenza vaccine development remains underexplored. In this study, we use the methylotrophic yeast Komagataella phaffii as a low-cost, industrial-scale platform to produce hemagglutinin-1 (HA1) subunits with programmable N -/ O -linked glycosylation. The methanol-utilization-slow (Mut S ) phenotype strain secreted 1.21 g/L HA1, and compared with the standard methanol-utilization-plus (Mut + ) phenotype strain, the N -linked and O -linked glycans were significantly reduced [liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS)/MS glycopeptide profile]. Despite hypoglycosylation, the antigen retained native conformation, binding H7-specific mAb Q74 with a K D of 1.34 × 10 –7 M. SpyTag/SpyCatcher-directed conjugation to ferritin drove quantitative self-assembly into 30 nm virus-like nanoparticles. Formulated with CpG-ODN 1826, the HA1-Mut S -ferritin candidate elicited Hemagglutination inhibition (HI) titers of 6.7 log 2 in specific pathogen-free (SPF) leghorns at 28 days post-immunization (dpi), significantly enhancing HA1-specific IgY responses ( p < 0.0001) while sustaining high-level circulating CD4 + T cells. At 28 dpi, chickens were challenged with 10 6 embryo infectious dose (EID) 50 of H7N9 avian influenza virus; the formulation conferred 100% clinical protection and accelerated viral clearance, matching the performance of conventional inactivated vaccines. Yeast-based processes significantly reduce downstream purification costs and eliminate reliance on chicken embryos, providing a scalable and biosafe platform for rapid avian influenza control.

title: H5N1 Marker Watch: Antiviral-Resistance and Mammalian-Adaptation Markers in Public U.S. Influenza A(H5N1) Sequences, Alongside CDC Wastewater H5 Detections
abstract: Public genomic and wastewater surveillance data for highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in the United States are open, large, and held in systems that do not speak to one another. We describe H5N1 Marker Watch, an open dataset that tabulates published antiviral-resistance and mammalian-adaptation marker positions in publicly deposited U.S. A(H5N1) protein sequences by state, collection year and host group, and places those counts alongside CDC National Wastewater Surveillance System H5 detections for the same state and year. Version 1.0.0 covers 95,582 protein sequences from 18,378 distinct isolates collected between 2022 and 2026 across 52 states and territories, screened at 36 marker positions drawn from WHO and CDC sources, producing 688,287 individual calls, joined to 124,427 wastewater results from 49 states of which 3,010 detected H5. Markers associated with reduced susceptibility to clinically used antivirals are rare: the neuraminidase substitution H275Y, the one substitution WHO identifies as a known clinical resistance marker, appears in 7 of 19,141 covering sequences (0.037%). The mammalian-adaptation picture differs: PB2 E627K rises across the period, from 0.126% of covering sequences in 2022 to 5.18% in the partial year 2026, while two further markers sit at frequencies better read as fixed features of the circulating clade. We report a methodological finding of general relevance: published marker positions arrive in several numbering conventions and some sources list the same site twice under two of them, so every position is validated against a named reference before it is counted. 11 of 36 markers required a numbering translation and 3 proved to be duplicates. Marker status throughout is genotype, not confirmed phenotype; no susceptibility testing was performed or is implied. Data, code and documentation are released openly and the pipeline is built for annual refresh.

title: Silent travelers: the potential of migratory birds and their ticks to introduce emerging viruses into Switzerland
abstract: Switzerland hosts over 400 bird species, many of which are migratory. Through diverse movement patterns, ranging from short distances to almost global migrations, these birds can introduce zoonotic viruses, such as West Nile virus (WNV) or avian influenza virus (AIV), as well as unknown and potentially emerging viruses. Furthermore, they facilitate the global dispersal of infected ectoparasites, particularly ticks, risking the introduction of novel tick-borne diseases. To assess this risk, we sampled 42 bird species (39 migratory, 3 resident) over seven months in 2023 at the Bolle di Magadino nature reserve and the Piano di Magadino area in the canton Ticino (Switzerland). This region, because of its transitional climate, serves as an important resting and breeding ground for migratory birds. In total, 496 oropharyngeal-cloacal swabs, 164 sera, and 22 associated ticks were collected. While RT-qPCR of the swabs detected no active WNV or AIV infections, ELISA testing identified Orthoflavivirus antibodies in 15 of 164 sera, indicating prior exposure. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing revealed a viral landscape spanning 33 families (29 of which were identified in birds). Within this virome, DNA viruses, predominantly Circoviridae, Genomoviridae, and Parvoviridae, dominated in abundance but exhibited low diversity. In contrast, the highly diverse RNA virome primarily reflected the birds’ dietary habits and the local habitat at the nature reserve. Notably, we report the first detection of Bole tick virus 4 (BoTV4) in Switzerland, identified in several ticks (Rhipicephalus turanicus) associated with long-distance migrants. This member of the newly established Pestiviridae family is already established in parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe. This study provides the first active surveillance of the wild bird virome in Switzerland. Our findings establish a framework for the early detection of emerging viruses and underscore the role of migratory birds as dispersal vectors for ticks and novel tick-borne viruses.

title: Defining influenza epidemic zones through temporal clustering of global surveillance data
abstract: Introduction: Modeling when influenza epidemics typically occur can help countries optimize surveillance, time clinical and public health interventions, and reduce the burden of influenza. Methods: We used influenza virus detections reported during 2011-2024 by 180 countries to the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System, excluding years impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2023). We analyzed data by calendar year (week 1-52) or shifted year (week 30-29) time windows, based on when most influenza detections occurred in each country. For countries with sufficient data, we computed generalized additive models (GAMs) of each country's weekly influenza-positive tests to smooth and impute time series distributions. From these GAMs, we calculated each country's weekly influenza burden. Country-specific time series were grouped using ensemble consensus k-means clustering, reducing the Euclidean distance between time series within clusters. We calculated cluster-specific GAMs to estimate average seasonal timing. Countries without sufficient data were assigned to a cluster based on population-weighted latitudinal distance to a cluster's mean latitude. Results: We identified five clusters, or epidemic zones, from 111 countries with sufficient data. The influenza burden in epidemic zones A and B was consistent with a northern hemisphere pattern, with most influenza detections occurring during November-May, while epidemic zones D and E were characterized by southern hemisphere-like seasonal timing, with most influenza burden occurring during June-November (D) and May-November (E). Epidemic zone C had most influenza burden occurring during September-March ; most countries assigned to this cluster were in the tropics. Conclusion: Epidemic zones may serve as a useful tool to strengthen and optimize influenza surveillance for global health decision-making (e.g., during vaccine strain composition discussions) and to guide country preparedness efforts for seasonal influenza epidemics, including timing enhanced surveillance and informing the availability of prevention and control efforts.

title_zh: 通过全球 监测 数据的时间聚类定义流感流行区
source_body_en: Introduction: Modeling when influenza epidemics typically occur can help countries optimize surveillance, time clinical and public health interventions, and reduce the burden of influenza. Methods: We used influenza virus detections reported during 2011-2024 by 180 countries to the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System, excluding years impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2023). We analyzed data by calendar year (week 1-52) or shifted year (week 30-29) time windows, based on when most influenza detections occurred in each country. For countries with sufficient data, we computed generalized additive models (GAMs) of each country's weekly influenza-positive tests to smooth and impute time series distributions. From these GAMs, we calculated each country's weekly influenza burden. Country-specific time series were grouped using ensemble consensus k-means clustering, reducing the Euclidean distance between time series within clusters. We calculated cluster-specific GAMs to estimate average seasonal timing. Countries without sufficient data were assigned to a cluster based on population-weighted latitudinal distance to a cluster's mean latitude. Results: We identified five clusters, or epidemic zones, from 111 countries with sufficient data. The influenza burden in epidemic zones A and B was consistent with a northern hemisphere pattern, with most influenza detections occurring during November-May, while epidemic zones D and E were characterized by southern hemisphere-like seasonal timing, with most influenza burden occurring during June-November (D) and May-November (E). Epidemic zone C had most influenza burden occurring during September-March ; most countries assigned to this cluster were in the tropics. Conclusion: Epidemic zones may serve as a useful tool to strengthen and optimize influenza surveillance for global health decision-making (e.g., during vaccine strain composition discussions) and to guide country preparedness efforts for seasonal influenza epidemics, including timing enhanced surveillance and informing the availability of prevention and control efforts.
abstract_zh: 简介:对流感流行通常发生的时间进行建模可以帮助各国优化 监测、安排临床和公共卫生干预措施并减轻流感负担。方法:我们使用了 2011-2024 年期间 180 个国家向全球流感 监测 和响应系统报告的流感病毒检测结果,不包括受 COVID-19 大流行影响的年份(2020-2023 年)。我们根据每个国家大多数流感检测发生的时间,按日历年(第 1-52 周)或轮班年(第 30-29 周)时间窗口分析数据。对于拥有足够数据的国家,我们计算了每个国家每周流感阳性检测的广义加性模型(GAM),以平滑和估算时间序列分布。根据这些 GAM,我们计算了每个国家每周的流感负担。使用集成共识 k 均值聚类对特定国家/地区的时间序列进行分组,从而减少聚类内时间序列之间的欧几里得距离。我们计算了特定于集群的 GAM 来估计平均季节性时间。没有足够数据的国家根据人口加权纬度与聚类平均纬度的距离分配到一个聚类。结果:我们在数据充足的 111 个国家中确定了 5 个集群或流行区。A区和B区的流感负担与北半球模式一致,大部分流感检测发生在11月至5月;而D区和E区则具有类似南半球的季节性时间特征,大部分流感负担发生在6月至11月(D)和5月至11月(E)。C区流感负担主要发生在9月-3月;大多数分配到该组的国家都位于热带地区。结论:流行区可以作为加强和优化流感 监测 的有用工具,以促进全球卫生决策(例如,在 疫苗 毒株组成讨论期间),并指导各国针对 季节性流感 流行病的准备工作,包括加强 监测 的时间安排和通报预防和控制工作的可用性。

title: Comparative immunogenicity of several inactivated influenza vaccines among healthcare workers in Hong Kong
abstract: We compared the immunogenicity of three licensed egg-based inactivated influenza vaccines, including TetrAnflu (Sinovac quadrivalent), Fluarix Tetra (GSK quadrivalent), and Vaxigrip (Sanofi trivalent), in adult healthcare workers in Hong Kong during the 2025/26 season. Age- and sex-matched recipients (n=30-40 per group) with paired pre- and post-vaccination sera were identified from an ongoing cohort. Hemagglutination-inhibition assays were performed against the egg-propagated 2025/26 vaccine reference strains. The three vaccines induced broadly comparable geometric mean fold-rises, post-vaccination geometric mean titers, proportions achieving titers >=40, and seroconversion rates against vaccine strains. These real-world data support the interchangeability of the three products for seasonal influenza vaccination programs among healthcare workers.

title_zh: 香港医护人员中几种灭活流感 疫苗 的免疫原性比较
source_body_en: We compared the immunogenicity of three licensed egg-based inactivated influenza vaccines, including TetrAnflu (Sinovac quadrivalent), Fluarix Tetra (GSK quadrivalent), and Vaxigrip (Sanofi trivalent), in adult healthcare workers in Hong Kong during the 2025/26 season. Age- and sex-matched recipients (n=30-40 per group) with paired pre- and post-vaccination sera were identified from an ongoing cohort. Hemagglutination-inhibition assays were performed against the egg-propagated 2025/26 vaccine reference strains. The three vaccines induced broadly comparable geometric mean fold-rises, post-vaccination geometric mean titers, proportions achieving titers >=40, and seroconversion rates against vaccine strains. These real-world data support the interchangeability of the three products for seasonal influenza vaccination programs among healthcare workers.

title: Defective Viral Genomes Reveal History-dependent Self-regulation of Type I Interferon Dynamics
abstract: Type I interferons (IFN) help clear a viral infection, but IFN levels can then decline to reset the antiviral state and avoid innate immune dysregulation. Such dysregulation can occur following infection with highly pathogenic and pandemic RNA viruses, such as H5N1 influenza A viruses or SARS-CoV-2. In spite of the strong innate immune response that these viruses induce, pandemic viruses replicate and spread successfully, suggesting that they can circumvent the effects of IFN. Innate immune activation is triggered when host cells detect viral RNA, especially defective viral genomes (DVGs). A strong IFN response (e.g. to DVGs or a highly immunogenic wild-type infection) must then decline through negative feedback involving the IFN receptor. How DVGs modulate this feedback remains poorly understood. To quantify positive and negative IFN regulation, we first performed in vitro experiments combining different doses of viral RNA and exogenous IFN, and measured subsequent IFN expression. We next developed an in vivo Bayesian computational model that captures the impact of influenza virus DVGs on both positive and negative IFN feedback. Competition between DVGs and virus is also considered. Finally, we calibrated this model on published in vitro and in vivo influenza virus infection data. Our model suggests that the cumulative IFN exposure of a host cell, rather than the instantaneous IFN level, shapes further IFN induction; this gives DVGs a dual role: beyond triggering IFN induction, they can also lower it through negative feedback. Our model further predicts that these effects are important locally, shaping the spatial dynamics of the response, allowing suppression of innate immune responses in neighbouring, uninfected cells. Through this model, we can explain two important biological observations: i) IFN levels can decline while virus and DVG levels continue to rise in tissue culture and mouse infections; and ii) pandemic viruses that produce high levels of immunogenic RNA molecules can successfully replicate through local innate immune suppression. Overall, we propose that heterogeneity within viral populations (including DVGs and other noncanonical viral RNAs) can modulate positive and negative feedback loops and shape infection outcomes. More broadly, our work may support studies into the therapeutic use of these viral RNA populations.

title: Structure-based virtual screening of cyanobacterial metabolites against key influenza A virus targets
abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) remains a major threat to global health and livestock industries, necessitating the discovery of new antiviral agents. In this study, a structure-based virtual screening of 1288 cyanobacterial secondary metabolites was performed against key IAV proteins, including hemagglutinin (H3 and H5), neuraminidase (N1 and N2), and RNA polymerase subunits (PB2 and PA). Molecular docking was conducted using AutoDock Vina with a rigid receptor–flexible ligand approach, and binding conformations were evaluated based on docking scores, molecular size, binding orientation, and interactions with functionally critical residues. A multi-target docking strategy combined with multiple docking-related criteria identified several promising candidates with more favorable predicted docking scores than the corresponding native ligands for H3, H5, N1, and N2, but slightly less favorable scores for PB2 and PA. Key compounds included 11,12-didehydrospironostoic acid, 7-formyl-3-methoxy-5-methylindanone, mycosporine-glycine-alanine, palythine-serine, Asterina-330, toyocamycin, usujirene, tjipanazole derivatives, tubercidin, and didmolamide A. Notably, among the prioritized compounds, metabolites from Calothrix exhibited the broadest predicted multi-target binding profile, followed by Tolypothrix , while compounds derived from Lyngbya/Moorea , Scytonema , Leptolyngbya , Nostoc , and Fischerella demonstrated target-specific or limited multi-target binding profiles. Scaffold-based analysis revealed key structural classes, including nucleoside-like compounds, mycosporine-like amino acids, and peptide/alkaloid derivatives, contributing to favorable predicted binding interactions with functionally critical residues. ADMET evaluation revealed variable predicted pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles among the prioritized compounds, with several candidates exhibiting low predicted intestinal absorption or elevated mutagenicity risk, highlighting the need for further safety and pharmacokinetic evaluation. Overall, this study highlights cyanobacterial metabolites as a structurally diverse and underexplored source of potential multi-target antiviral candidates against IAV and provides a framework for future computational refinement and experimental validation toward applications in both human and animal health.

source_body_en: Influenza A virus (IAV) remains a major threat to global health and livestock industries, necessitating the discovery of new antiviral agents. In this study, a structure-based virtual screening of 1288 cyanobacterial secondary metabolites was performed against key IAV proteins, including hemagglutinin (H3 and H5), neuraminidase (N1 and N2), and RNA polymerase subunits (PB2 and PA). Molecular docking was conducted using AutoDock Vina with a rigid receptor–flexible ligand approach, and binding conformations were evaluated based on docking scores, molecular size, binding orientation, and interactions with functionally critical residues. A multi-target docking strategy combined with multiple docking-related criteria identified several promising candidates with more favorable predicted docking scores than the corresponding native ligands for H3, H5, N1, and N2, but slightly less favorable scores for PB2 and PA. Key compounds included 11,12-didehydrospironostoic acid, 7-formyl-3-methoxy-5-methylindanone, mycosporine-glycine-alanine, palythine-serine, Asterina-330, toyocamycin, usujirene, tjipanazole derivatives, tubercidin, and didmolamide A. Notably, among the prioritized compounds, metabolites from Calothrix exhibited the broadest predicted multi-target binding profile, followed by Tolypothrix , while compounds derived from Lyngbya/Moorea , Scytonema , Leptolyngbya , Nostoc , and Fischerella demonstrated target-specific or limited multi-target binding profiles. Scaffold-based analysis revealed key structural classes, including nucleoside-like compounds, mycosporine-like amino acids, and peptide/alkaloid derivatives, contributing to favorable predicted binding interactions with functionally critical residues. ADMET evaluation revealed variable predicted pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles among the prioritized compounds, with several candidates exhibiting low predicted intestinal absorption or elevated mutagenicity risk, highlighting the need for further safety and pharmacokinetic evaluation. Overall, this study highlights cyanobacterial metabolites as a structurally diverse and underexplored source of potential multi-target antiviral candidates against IAV and provides a framework for future computational refinement and experimental validation toward applications in both human and animal health.
abstract_zh: 甲型流感病毒 (IAV) 仍然是全球健康和畜牧业的主要威胁,因此需要发现新的 抗病毒药物 制剂。在这项研究中,针对关键 IAV 蛋白,包括血凝素(H3 和 H5)、神经氨酸酶(N1 和 N2)和 RNA 聚合酶亚基(PB2 和 PA),对 1288 种蓝藻次生代谢物进行了基于结构的虚拟筛选。使用 AutoDock Vina 和刚性受体-柔性配体方法进行分子对接,并根据对接分数、分子大小、结合方向以及与功能关键残基的相互作用来评估结合构象。多目标对接策略与多个对接相关标准相结合,确定了几种有前途的候选物,其预测对接分数比 H3、H5、N1 和 N2 的相应天然配体更有利,但 PB2 和 PA 的分数稍差。主要化合物包括 11,12-二脱氢螺菌酸、7-甲酰基-3-甲氧基-5-甲基茚满酮、菌孢素-甘氨酸-丙氨酸、palythine-丝氨酸、Asterina-330、丰加霉素、usujirene、tjipanaz 衍生物、结核菌素和去甲酰胺 A。值得注意的是,在优先化合物中,来自 Calothrix 的代谢物表现出预测的多靶点结合谱最广泛,其次是 Tolypothrix,而源自 Lyngbya/Moorea、Scytonema、Leptolyngbya、Nostoc 和 Fischerella 的化合物则表现出靶点特异性或有限的多靶点结合谱。基于支架的分析揭示了关键的结构类别,包括核苷样化合物、菌孢素样氨基酸和肽/生物碱衍生物,有助于预测与功能关键残基的良好预测结合相互作用。ADMET 评估揭示了优先化合物中不同的预测药代动力学和毒性特征,其中几种候选化合物表现出预测肠道吸收低或致突变风险升高,这突出表明需要进一步进行安全性和药代动力学评估。总体而言,这项研究强调蓝藻代谢物是一种结构多样且尚未充分开发的抗 IAV 潜在多靶点 抗病毒药物 候选物的来源,并为未来计算细化和实验验证在人类和动物健康方面的应用提供了框架。

full_text: AbstractObjectiveTo evaluate the immunogenicity and safety of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV3) in adults aged ≥18 years living with HIV and to provide evidence supporting influenza vaccination in this population in China.MethodsThis single-center, open-label comparative analysis was derived from a larger three-arm clinical study. For the present comparative analysis, 472 vaccinated participants were planned, including 236 adults living with HIV (Group 1) and 236 age- and sex-comparable HIV-uninfected adults (Group 2). Participants in both groups received one dose of IIV3 (0.5 mL) on Day 0. Blood samples were collected before and 28 days after vaccination for hemagglutination inhibition (HI) antibody testing against A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B/Victoria strains. Immunogenicity endpoints included seroconversion rate, seroprotection rate, geometric mean titer (GMT), and geometric mean increase (GMI). Safety was assessed by monitoring solicited and unsolicited adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) during 6 months of follow-up. An unvaccinated cohort of adults living with HIV from the original trial was included only for an exploratory, descriptive analysis of influenza-like illness (ILI), without assessment of vaccine efficacy.ResultsA total of 489 participants were enrolled, including 237 in Group 1 and 252 in Group 2. At 28 days post-vaccination, seroconversion rates did not differ significantly between Group 1 and Group 2 for A(H1N1) (91.00% vs. 86.69%, P > 0.05), but significantly lower for A(H3N2) (49.50% vs. 89.52%) and B/Victoria (40.00% vs. 64.52%) (both P < 0.001). Seroprotection rates were also lower in Group 1 than in Group 2 for A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B/Victoria (94.00% vs. 97.98%, 63.50% vs. 97.18%, and 40.50% vs. 68.55%, respectively). Post-vaccination GMTs were significantly lower in Group 1 for all three strains (all P < 0.001). GMI was higher for A(H1N1) but lower for A(H3N2) and B/Victoria in Group 1 than in Group 2 (all P < 0.001). Multivariable analyses showed that HIV infection remained independently associated with several measures of vaccine-induced immune responses after adjustment for demographic and clinical factors, particularly for A(H3N2). IIV3 was generally safe and well tolerated. Most AEs were mild in severity, and no Grade 4 adverse reactions or vaccine-related SAEs were reported. During the period from 29 days to 6 months after vaccination, few influenza-like illness events were reported among vaccinated and unvaccinated participants living with HIV; these findings were descriptive and were not used to assess vaccine efficacy against influenza.ConclusionAdults living with HIV developed substantial antibody responses following IIV3 vaccination, although the magnitude of response varied across influenza strains. A(H1N1) seroconversion was high in adults living with HIV, whereas responses to A(H3N2) and B/Victoria were generally lower than those in HIV-uninfected adults. HIV infection remained associated with reduced vaccine-induced immune responses for several strain-specific outcomes after multivariable adjustment, with associations particularly evident for A(H3N2). IIV3 was safe and well tolerated, supporting current recommendations for influenza vaccination in adults living with HIV.Clinical trial registrationhttps://www.chictr.org.cn/showprojEN.html?proj=255613, identifier ChiCTR2500112191.Keywords: HIV infection, immunogenicity, safety, seroprotection, trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine MethodsStudy design and participantsThis study was a single-center, open-label comparative analysis derived from a larger three-arm clinical study conducted in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China, in which participants living with HIV were randomized to vaccination or no vaccination. Participant recruitment was conducted at Hangzhou Xixi Hospital of Hangzhou Medical College and three community health service centers in Xihu District, Hangzhou. Participants living with HIV and HIV-uninfected participants were enrolled concurrently during the same study period. The present analysis evaluated the immunogenicity and safety of IIV3 in adults living with HIV and compared vaccine-induced immune responses with those in an age- and sex-comparable group of HIV-uninfected adults.For the present comparative analysis, 472 vaccinated participants were planned, including 236 adults living with HIV (Group 1) and 236 age- and sex-comparable HIV-uninfected adults (Group 2). Participants living with HIV were stratified by age (18–49 years and ≥50 years) and recruited primarily from the study hospital, whereas HIV-uninfected adults were recruited from both hospital- and community-based settings. Group 2 was selected to be age- and sex-comparable to Group 1 without individual matching. All participants included in the present analysis received a single 0.5 mL dose of IIV3 administered intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle on Day 0.Blood samples were collected before vaccination (Day 0) and 28 days after vaccination to assess HI antibody responses. Participants were provided with diary cards to record adverse events (AEs) following vaccination. Solicited and unsolicited AEs were monitored after vaccination, and serious adverse events (SAEs) were collected throughout the 6-month follow-up period.The original trial also included an unvaccinated cohort of adults living with HIV. Data from this cohort were used only for an exploratory, descriptive analysis of influenza-like illness (ILI) during follow-up. Because ILI was not virologically confirmed, this analysis was considered hypothesis-generating and was not intended to assess vaccine efficacy against influenza. At the time of study conduct, seasonal influenza vaccination in China was voluntary and outside the National Immunization Program. Chinese technical guidelines recommended annual influenza vaccination for all individuals aged ≥6 months without contraindications, with priority given to key and high-risk populations (9). The inclusion of the unvaccinated group of adults living with HIV was considered in this policy context, and randomization concerned receipt of the study influenza vaccine only without affecting routine HIV care or antiretroviral therapy. The parent study protocol was approved by the relevant ethics committees, and all participants provided written informed consent.Participants included in the present analysis were adults aged ≥18 years who had not received any influenza vaccine within the year preceding enrollment and had a body temperature <37.3 °C at enrollment. Female participants of childbearing potential were required to use effective contraception and have no pregnancy plans during the study period.Key exclusion criteria included a history of severe allergic reactions to influenza vaccines or vaccine components, pregnancy or breastfeeding, use of immunosuppressive agents within 1 month before enrollment, receipt of blood products or immunoglobulins within 3 months before enrollment, acute febrile illness, Guillain–Barré syndrome, coagulation disorders contraindicating intramuscular injection, or any condition that, in the investigator’s judgment, could interfere with study assessments.Study endpointsThe primary endpoint was the seroconversion rate against influenza A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B/Victoria strains in Group 1 at 28 days after vaccination. Secondary endpoints included comparisons of seroconversion rates, seroprotection rates, GMTs, and GMIs between Group 1 and Group 2. Exploratory endpoints included evaluation of demographic and clinical factors associated with vaccine-induced immune responses. Additional analyses among participants living with HIV evaluated recent CD4+ T-cell count, time since HIV diagnosis, and duration of ART. Safety endpoints included AEs and SAEs following vaccination. ILI occurrence was also summarized descriptively as an exploratory, hypothesis-generating observation among vaccinated and unvaccinated participants living with HIV. ILI was defined as fever (≥38.0 °C) accompanied by cough or sore throat. ILI was identified based on clinical symptoms without virological confirmation and was therefore not used to assess vaccine efficacy against influenza.Sample size calculation and randomizationThis analysis was derived from a larger three-arm, single-center, open-label clinical study. The original sample size was calculated assuming seroconversion rates of 40% and 23% in vaccinated and unvaccinated adults living with HIV, respectively. With a two-sided α of 0.05, 95% power, and an anticipated dropout rate of 18%, 236 participants were required per group.In the original trial, participants living with HIV were stratified by age (18–49 years and ≥50 years) and randomly assigned to either the vaccinated or unvaccinated group using a stratified randomization sequence generated with SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA). HIV-uninfected adults were enrolled separately as an age- and sex-comparable comparison group. For the present analysis, only vaccinated adults living with HIV and vaccinated HIV-uninfected adults were included.Study vaccineThe IIV3 (Shipulier®) was manufactured by Changchun Institute of Biological Products Co., Ltd. (Changchun, China). Each dose (0.5 mL per vial, batch number: TA20240725, expiration date: July 17, 2025) contained 15 μg of hemagglutinin antigen from each influenza virus strain included in the vaccine formulation. The IIV3 formulation corresponded to the WHO-recommended egg-based trivalent influenza vaccine composition for the 2024–2025 Northern Hemisphere season (10).Immunogenicity assessmentImmunogenicity was evaluated using the hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay performed at the Bioanalytical Center of Chongqing Meilaide Biopharmaceutical Co., Ltd. Serum HI antibody titers against influenza A(H1N1) (A/Victoria/4897/2022), A(H3N2) (A/Thailand/8/2022), and B/Victoria (B/Austria/1359417/2021) vaccine strains were measured before vaccination (Day 0) and 28 days after vaccination.Immunogenicity endpoints included seroconversion rate, seroprotection rate, GMTs, and GMIs. Seroconversion was defined as a pre-vaccination HI antibody titer <1:10 and a post-vaccination titer ≥1:40, or a pre-vaccination titer ≥1:10 with at least a four-fold increase after vaccination. Seroconversion rate was defined as the proportion of participants who achieved seroconversion. Seroprotection was defined as an HI antibody titer ≥1:40, and the seroprotection rate was defined as the proportion of participants achieving this threshold at the specified time point. GMTs were calculated for each influenza strain before and 28 days after vaccination. GMI was calculated as the geometric mean of the individual post-vaccination-to-pre-vaccination HI antibody titer ratios.Safety assessmentSafety assessments included all solicited and unsolicited AEs, regardless of their relationship to vaccination. Participants were observed for 30 minutes after vaccination and were provided with diary cards to record AEs occurring within 28 days after vaccination. Solicited local (injection-site pain, induration, swelling, rash, erythema, and pruritus) and systemic (fever, cough, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and acute allergic reactions) AEs were collected during the first 7 days following vaccination. Any medical occurrence other than the predefined solicited events was recorded as an unsolicited AE through Day 28. SAEs were monitored for 6 months through active surveillance, consisting of scheduled on-site or telephone follow-up every 7 days, supplemented by spontaneous reporting from participants.Safety analyses compared the incidence, severity, and causality of AEs, as well as the incidence of SAEs, between Group 1 and Group 2. All reported AEs were graded for severity and assessed for causality by trained investigators according to the Guiding Principles for Grading Adverse Reactions in Clinical Trials of Preventive Vaccines (NMPA No. 102, 2019) (11).For participants living with HIV, planned hospitalizations or hospitalizations for routine clinical management that were scheduled before enrollment and did not reflect a worsening medical condition were not classified as SAEs, in accordance with the study protocol. All other events meeting the protocol-defined SAE criteria were reported and evaluated by the investigators.Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA). GMTs, GMIs, and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated from log10-transformed HI antibody titers and back-transformed for presentation. Seroconversion and seroprotection rates were calculated with corresponding 95% CIs. Comparisons between groups were performed using the chi-square test, Fisher’s exact test, or t-test, as appropriate. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to identify factors associated with seroconversion and seroprotection, whereas multivariable linear regression analyses were performed using individual-level log2-transformed post-vaccination HI antibody titers and log2-transformed antibody fold increases as continuous outcomes. Separate models were fitted for each influenza strain. Among vaccinated participants living with HIV and HIV-uninfected participants, models included age (18–49 vs. ≥50 years), sex, HIV infection status, comorbidity, and baseline log2 HI antibody titer. In exploratory analyses restricted to vaccinated participants living with HIV, models included age, sex, comorbidity, baseline log2 HI antibody titer, recent CD4+ T-cell count (<500 vs. ≥500 cells/μL), time since HIV diagnosis (<5 vs. ≥5 years), and duration of ART (<2 vs. ≥2 years). Baseline log2 HI antibody titer was modeled as a continuous variable.As a complementary analysis of the overall humoral response across the three vaccine strains, a global three-strain response score was constructed using an approach adapted from Tawfik et al. (12). HI titers for A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B/Victoria were transformed into ordinal scores, combined with a seroprotection-weighting component, and normalized using an ordered quantile (ORQ) transformation. A repeated-measures linear mixed-effects model was fitted with the global response score as the outcome, Group, Time, and Group × Time as fixed effects, and participant as a random intercept. At Day 28, the distribution of the number of strains achieving seroprotection (HI ≥1:40; 0–3 strains) was compared between groups using the Pearson chi-square test, and the proportion achieving seroprotection against all three strains was compared using the Pearson chi-square test with Yates’ continuity correction. The complementary global-response analyses were performed using Python version 3.12.All statistical tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.Analysis setsThe full analysis set (FAS) included all vaccinated participants with evaluable pre- and post-vaccination HI antibody results. The per-protocol set (PPS) included participants who completed the study without major protocol deviations and had evaluable immunogenicity data at both study visits. Safety analyses were performed using the safety set (SS), which included all vaccinated participants. full_text_sections.methods: MethodsStudy design and participantsThis study was a single-center, open-label comparative analysis derived from a larger three-arm clinical study conducted in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China, in which participants living with HIV were randomized to vaccination or no vaccination. Participant recruitment was conducted at Hangzhou Xixi Hospital of Hangzhou Medical College and three community health service centers in Xihu District, Hangzhou. Participants living with HIV and HIV-uninfected participants were enrolled concurrently during the same study period. Participants living with HIV were stratified by age (18–49 years and ≥50 years) and recruited primarily from the study hospital, whereas HIV-uninfected adults were recruited from both hospital- and community-based settings. Group 2 was selected to be age- and sex-comparable to Group 1 without individual matching. All participants included in the present analysis received a single 0.5 mL dose of IIV3 administered intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle on Day 0.Blood samples were collected before vaccination (Day 0) and 28 days after vaccination to assess HI antibody responses. Participants were provided with diary cards to record adverse events (AEs) following vaccination. Solicited and unsolicited AEs were monitored after vaccination, and serious adverse events (SAEs) were collected throughout the 6-month follow-up period.The original trial also included an unvaccinated cohort of adults living with HIV. Data from this cohort were used only for an exploratory, descriptive analysis of influenza-like illness (ILI) during follow-up. Because ILI was not virologically confirmed, this analysis was considered hypothesis-generating and was not intended to assess vaccine efficacy against influenza. At the time of study conduct, seasonal influenza vaccination in China was voluntary and outside the National Immunization Program. Chinese technical guidelines recommended annual influenza vaccination for all individuals aged ≥6 months without contraindications, with priority given to key and high-risk populations (9). The parent study protocol was approved by the relevant ethics committees, and all participants provided written informed consent.Participants included in the present analysis were adults aged ≥18 years who had not received any influenza vaccine within the year preceding enrollment and had a body temperature <37.3 °C at enrollment. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionSeasonal influenza remains an important cause of morbidity in adults living with HIV, and international guidelines recommend annual influenza vaccination for people living with HIV (6, 13). Previous systematic reviews have shown that influenza vaccines are generally safe and immunogenic in adults living with HIV, although immune responses vary across influenza strains and study populations (5, 14). More recently, a Chinese comparative study reported satisfactory antibody responses following quadrivalent influenza vaccination but lower immunogenicity among individuals with lower CD4+ T-cell counts (15). Our study extends these findings by providing contemporary evidence on the immunogenicity and safety of IIV3 in Chinese adults living with HIV and demonstrating strain-specific differences in vaccine-induced immune responses compared with HIV-uninfected adults.The most important finding of this study was the marked strain-specific variation in vaccine-induced immune responses. Although seroconversion against A(H1N1) was high in adults living with HIV and did not differ significantly between groups, antibody responses to A(H3N2) and B/Victoria were generally lower in adults living with HIV than in HIV-uninfected adults. Similar findings have been reported previously, particularly for A(H3N2) (5, 15). These strain-specific differences may reflect a combination of host-, virus-, and exposure-related factors rather than HIV-associated immune dysfunction alone. Several mechanisms may contribute to the observed differences. Chronic HIV infection is associated with persistent immune activation and impaired B-cell and T follicular helper cell function, which may compromise high-quality antibody production despite effective ART (16, 17). In addition, A(H3N2) viruses undergo frequent antigenic drift, resulting in substantial antigenic diversity and contributing to the lower and more variable vaccine effectiveness observed for A(H3N2) than for other influenza subtypes (18, 19). Vaccine strain composition may also be relevant. Compared with the 2023–2024 Northern Hemisphere season, the A(H3N2) component of egg-based vaccines was updated from an A/Darwin/9/2021-like virus to an A/Thailand/8/2022-like virus for the 2024–2025 season, whereas the A(H1N1)pdm09 and B/Victoria components remained unchanged (10, 20). The recent update of the A(H3N2) vaccine component indicates that differences in prior antigenic exposure and pre-existing immunity may be relevant when interpreting the strain-specific responses. However, because both groups received the same vaccine and HI responses were assessed against homologous vaccine strains, antigenic drift alone is unlikely to explain the between-group differences. The unchanged B/Victoria component further suggests that recent vaccine-strain updating cannot account for all of the observed strain-specific variation. Accordingly, the comparatively lower responses to A(H3N2) and B/Victoria likely reflect multiple contributing factors, and the relative contribution of HIV-associated immune dysfunction cannot be determined from the present study. These strain-specific findings should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating and require confirmation across multiple influenza seasons and independent cohorts.The complementary global three-strain analysis provided an integrated assessment of humoral responses across the three vaccine strains. Although global response scores were lower in participants living with HIV at both Day 0 and Day 28, the Group × Time interaction was not statistically significant, indicating that the magnitude of increase from baseline did not differ significantly between groups in the primary global-response analysis. Notably, the lower global response observed in adults living with HIV at baseline persisted at Day 28, as confirmed by the model-based between-group contrast. In contrast, Tawfik et al. reported that the baseline difference between previously unvaccinated and vaccinated healthy adults was no longer significant by Day 90 (12), although direct comparison is limited by differences in study populations and assessment time points. Consistent with the global response findings, a substantially lower proportion of participants living with HIV achieved seroprotection against all three vaccine strains at Day 28. Together with the strain-specific analyses, the global three-strain assessment provides an integrated view of humoral immunity, showing that both groups mounted substantial antibody responses after vaccination, while between-group differences in the overall level and breadth of responses remained evident.Beyond the descriptive comparisons, multivariable analyses demonstrated that HIV infection remained independently associated with reduced vaccine-induced immune responses after adjustment for demographic characteristics, comorbidity, and baseline HI antibody levels. This finding indicates that the reduced immunogenicity observed in adults living with HIV was not fully accounted for by the measured baseline characteristics or baseline HI antibody levels. These findings support continued efforts to better understand and optimize influenza vaccine responses in people living with HIV, particularly for strains showing comparatively lower immunogenicity.In exploratory analyses restricted to participants living with HIV, recent CD4+ T-cell count, time since HIV diagnosis, and ART duration were not independently associated with vaccine-induced immune responses after adjustment for other covariates. Previous studies have reported inconsistent associations between these HIV-related factors and influenza vaccine immunogenicity, with lower CD4+ T-cell counts more consistently linked to reduced immune responses, whereas evidence regarding ART duration remains limited (5, 15). The absence of significant associations in our study may reflect the relatively preserved immune status and well-controlled HIV infection in this cohort, in which all participants were receiving ART and all participants with evaluable HIV RNA were virologically suppressed (<200 copies/mL). In contrast, baseline HI antibody level was consistently associated with post-vaccination immune responses, suggesting an important role of pre-existing influenza immunity in short-term vaccine responses. These exploratory findings should be interpreted cautiously and require confirmation in larger and more diverse cohorts.Baseline HI antibody level was consistently associated with vaccine-induced antibody responses in both the overall and HIV-restricted analyses. Higher baseline antibody levels were associated with greater odds of achieving seroprotection and higher post-vaccination antibody titers but smaller antibody increases after vaccination. This pattern has been consistently reported in influenza vaccine studies and likely reflects a ceiling effect, whereby individuals with higher pre-existing immunity have less potential for further fold increases despite achieving higher absolute antibody titers (21, 22). These findings highlight the importance of accounting for baseline HI antibody levels when evaluating vaccine immunogenicity and support their inclusion as a continuous covariate in multivariable analyses.Older age was associated with reduced immune responses to A(H3N2) but enhanced responses to B/Victoria. Although immunosenescence is known to influence influenza vaccine immunogenicity, age-related effects vary across influenza strains and study populations (23, 24). Although age was a prespecified stratification factor, the study was not specifically powered to detect age-related differences in vaccine-induced immune responses. Therefore, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.Consistent with previous evidence, IIV3 was well tolerated in adults living with HIV, with no vaccine-related SAEs observed. full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionIn conclusion, adults living with HIV developed substantial antibody responses following IIV3 vaccination, although the magnitude of vaccine-induced immune responses varied across influenza strains. Compared with HIV-uninfected adults, adults living with HIV showed high seroconversion against A(H1N1), whereas immune responses to A(H3N2) and B/Victoria were generally lower. HIV infection remained independently associated with reduced vaccine-induced immune responses for several strain-specific outcomes after adjustment for demographic and clinical factors, although residual confounding from unmeasured factors cannot be excluded. Baseline HI antibody level was consistently associated with post-vaccination antibody responses. IIV3 demonstrated a favorable safety profile and was well tolerated in adults living with HIV. These findings provide contemporary evidence supporting annual influenza vaccination in adults living with HIV in China and highlight the importance of considering strain-specific differences when evaluating vaccine immunogenicity in this population. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are warranted to assess the durability of immune responses and their relationship with clinical protection.

title_original: Immunogenicity and safety of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine in adults living with HIV compared with HIV-uninfected adults: a study from China

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the immunogenicity and safety of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV3) in adults living with HIV compared with HIV-uninfected adults, addressing the knowledge gap about how HIV affects vaccine responses in this population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a single-center, open-label comparative analysis derived from a larger three-arm clinical study conducted in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China. It included 236 adults living with HIV (Group 1) and 236 age- and sex-comparable HIV-uninfected adults (Group 2).
analysis.methods: Immunogenicity was assessed using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) antibody testing against A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B/Victoria strains, with blood samples collected before and 28 days after vaccination. Safety was evaluated by monitoring adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) during 6 months of follow-up.
analysis.main_results: At 28 days post-vaccination, seroconversion rates did not differ significantly between Group 1 and Group 2 for A(H1N1), but were significantly lower in Group 1 for A(H3N2) and B/Victoria (all P < 0.001). Post-vaccination GMTs were also significantly lower in Group 1 for all three strains. Most AEs were mild, and no Grade 4 adverse reactions or vaccine-related SAEs were reported.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that adults living with HIV developed substantial antibody responses following IIV3 vaccination, although the magnitude of response varied across influenza strains, particularly for A(H3N2).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that IIV3 is safe and well tolerated in adults living with HIV, supporting current recommendations for influenza vaccination in this population, and highlight the need for further research on strain-specific immune responses in HIV-positive individuals.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the use of clinical symptoms to identify influenza-like illness (ILI) without virological confirmation, which precludes assessing vaccine efficacy. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the analysis and the lack of virological confirmation for ILI.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the immunogenicity and safety of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV3) in adults living with HIV compared to HIV-uninfected adults in China. The research aimed to address the knowledge gap regarding vaccine responses in HIV-positive individuals. A total of 489 participants were enrolled, with 237 in the HIV group and 252 in the uninfected group. Immunogenicity was measured using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assays against A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B/Victoria strains, while safety was assessed through monitoring adverse events. Results showed that seroconversion rates for A(H1N1) were similar between groups, but significantly lower for A(H3N2) and B/Victoria in the HIV group. Post-vaccination GMTs were also lower in the HIV group for all three strains. Most adverse events were mild, and no serious adverse events were reported. The authors concluded that adults living with HIV developed substantial antibody responses to IIV3, though the magnitude varied by strain. The study supports current vaccination recommendations for HIV-positive adults but has limitations due to the lack of virological confirmation for ILI, which affects the assessment of vaccine efficacy. The evidence is moderate in strength.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估三价灭活流感 疫苗 (IIV3) 在感染 HIV 的成人中与未感染 HIV 的成人相比的免疫原性和安全性,弥补有关 HIV 如何影响该人群中 疫苗 反应的知识差距。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一项单中心、开放标签的比较分析,源自于中国浙江省杭州市进行的一项更大规模的三组临床研究。其中包括 236 名感染艾滋病毒的成年人(第 1 组)和 236 名年龄和性别相当的未感染艾滋病毒的成年人(第 2 组)。

elements_zh.main_results: 疫苗接种 后 28 天,A(H1N1) 组 1 和组 2 之间的血清转化率没有显着差异,但 甲型H3N2流感病毒 和 B/Victoria 组 1 的血清转化率显着较低(所有 P < 0.001)。对于所有三种菌株,第 1 组中 疫苗接种 后的 GMT 也显着较低。大多数 AE 均为轻度,未报告 4 级不良反应或 疫苗 相关 SAE。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,感染艾滋病毒的成年人在 IIV3 疫苗接种 后产生了显着的抗体反应,尽管反应的程度因流感毒株而异,特别是 甲型H3N2流感病毒。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,IIV3 在成人 HIV 感染者中是安全且耐受性良好的,支持目前针对该人群的流感 疫苗接种 的建议,并强调需要对 HIV 阳性个体中的毒株特异性 免疫应答 进行进一步研究。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性包括在没有病毒学确认的情况下使用临床症状来识别流感样疾病(ILI),这妨碍了评估 疫苗 的疗效。由于分析的观察性质以及缺乏 ILI 的病毒学确认,证据是中等的。
